statement: Working together, Kai and Lena paint a fence in 6 hours. Kai alone would take 10 hours. Kai paints alone for 2 hours and then stops, and Lena finishes the fence on her own. How many hours does Lena paint?

choices.misconception: I took the 2 hours off the 6 hours they need together.
I worked out that 4/5 of the fence was left and took 4/5 of their 6 hours together.
I took the 2 hours off Kai's 10 hours, as if Lena painted at Kai's speed.
I found that Lena alone takes 15 hours for the whole fence and forgot that Kai had already painted part of it.

hints: Work out what fraction of the fence each person paints in one hour.
Rates add when people work together, so Lena's hourly rate is the joint rate minus Kai's. Then find how much of the fence is left after Kai's 2 hours and divide it by Lena's rate.
Together they paint 1/6 of the fence per hour and Kai paints 1/10, so Lena paints 1/6 - 1/10 = 1/15 per hour. Kai's 2 hours cover 1/5 of the fence.

solutions.reliable: Together they paint 1/6 of the fence per hour and Kai alone paints 1/10, so Lena paints 1/6 - 1/10 = 1/15 of the fence per hour. In 2 hours Kai paints 2/10 = 1/5 of the fence, leaving 4/5. At 1/15 per hour, Lena needs (4/5) / (1/15) = 12 hours. The transferable idea: turn times into rates, add or subtract the rates, and never add or subtract the times themselves.
solutions.elegant: Call the fence 30 units, a number both 6 and 10 divide. Together they paint 5 units an hour and Kai paints 3, so Lena paints 2. Kai's 2 hours give 6 units, and Lena's remaining 24 units take 12 hours.

whyOnTest: Work-rate questions test adding rates rather than times; subtracting hours directly is the trap most of these choices fall into.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
